hints: Focus on moles of nitrogen atoms, not just moles of the whole compound, since each formula holds a different number of N atoms.
Notice that 101.1 g of potassium nitrate is exactly 1 mol, so start by working out how many moles of N that gives you.
Use the fact that one mole of urea holds two moles of N to work out what mass of urea gives you that same amount of nitrogen.
walkthrough:
**Find moles of potassium nitrate**

Think of this as counting how many nitrogen atoms you have to match. First find $M_r$ of $\text{KNO}_3$.

$$M_r(\text{KNO}_3) = 39.1 + 14.0 + (3 \times 16.0) = 101.1$$

So moles of $\text{KNO}_3$:
$$n = \frac{101.1}{101.1} = 1.0 \text{ mol}$$

**Find moles of nitrogen to match**

Each $\text{KNO}_3$ has 1 N atom, so 1 mol of $\text{KNO}_3$ contains 1 mol of N atoms. That is the target amount.

$$n(\text{N needed}) = 1.0 \text{ mol}$$

**Find $M_r$ of urea and link to nitrogen**

Urea is $\text{CO(NH}_2)_2$. Count carefully, there are 2 N atoms per molecule.

$$M_r(\text{urea}) = 12.0 + 16.0 + (2 \times 14.0) + (4 \times 1.0) = 60.0$$

So 1 mol urea (60 g) contains 2 mol N.

**Calculate mass of urea needed**

You only need 1 mol of N, so you only need half a mole of urea.

$$n(\text{urea}) = \frac{1.0}{2} = 0.50 \text{ mol}$$
$$m = 0.50 \times 60.0 = 30 \text{ g}$$

options.A: 22 g is too small. It would give less than 0.5 mol of urea and therefore less than 1 mol of N. It may come from a faulty $M_r$ calculation.
options.B: 30 g is 0.5 mol of urea. Since each mole of urea provides 2 mol of N, 0.5 mol provides exactly 1 mol of N, matching the 1 mol of N in 101.1 g of $\text{KNO}_3$.
options.C: 44 g has no mole link here. It does not give 1 mol of N from urea and may come from mixing up masses of $\text{CO}_2$ or other species.
options.D: 60 g is 1 full mole of urea, which contains 2 mol of N. This is double what is needed. It is the trap of matching moles of compounds (1 mol to 1 mol) and forgetting urea has two nitrogens per formula.
